clue.text: Gastronomic accessory for which Sayers's Montague gets prize

parts.note: Montague Egg is the commercial-traveller sleuth in Dorothy L. Sayers's short stories
a cup is a trophy awarded as a prize

explanation.surface: A gourmet's gadget is the reward a fictional detective wins.
explanation.walkthrough: Montague Egg, a wine salesman who solves crimes, appears in Dorothy L. Sayers's short stories alongside her better-known Lord Peter Wimsey.
explanation.definitionFit: A small holder for a boiled egg is a piece of tableware, an accessory of the breakfast table.

clue.text: Mostly burn with anger, an attribute of Pagnol's father

indicators.note: mostly means the word for burn loses its final letter, leaving most of it

parts.note: to glow is to burn steadily without flame
ire is a literary word for anger

explanation.surface: A man burns with rage, a trait of a French author's father.
explanation.walkthrough: Marcel Pagnol's memoir is titled La Gloire de mon père, so the father's attribute is French for glory.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for glory is what Pagnol's memoir title attributes to his father.

clue.text: Where you'll see students rowing about marks?

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about
M stands for marks, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A question about where students argue over their grades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' tempts as quarrelling over marks; it is boating, on the river through Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The river through Cambridge is where college crews of undergraduates train and race.

clue.text: Underworld controller; what a dog!

definitions.meaning: the Roman god ruling the realm of the dead
the Disney cartoon hound, Mickey Mouse's pet

explanation.definitionFit: One name serves both the Roman ruler of Hades and Disney's cartoon bloodhound.

clue.text: Thrill at act which one may perform in Davos or Zermatt

definitions.text: which one may perform in Davos or Zermatt

parts.note: a kick is a thrill or buzz
a turn is a variety act on stage

explanation.surface: Something exciting happens at a show staged in Swiss resorts.
explanation.walkthrough: Davos and Zermatt are Swiss ski resorts; the answer is a skiing manoeuvre.
explanation.definitionFit: A standing about-face on skis is a manoeuvre skiers make on Swiss slopes.

clue.text: Hooley that could be seen at start of Khovanshchina

definitions.text: Hooley that could be seen at start of Khovanshchina

parts.words: Hooley that could be seen at start of Khovanshchina
parts.note: a hooley is a lively party; the clue imagines a raucous dance at the opening of Mussorgsky's opera

explanation.walkthrough: A knees-up is a British colloquial term for a boisterous party; Khovanshchina is Mussorgsky's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooley and this British term both mean a noisy, lively party with dancing.

clue.text: Clipper used to produce a short loose dress

parts.note: cutty is a Scots word meaning short
a sark is a Scots word for a shirt or loose shift

explanation.surface: A pair of scissors turns a garment into a short smock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clipper' suggests scissors; it is the famous tea clipper ship, named from the short shift in Burns's poem Tam o' Shanter.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous nineteenth-century tea ship preserved at Greenwich is a fast sailing vessel of the clipper type.

clue.text: Horseman at end of night getting smashed!

definitions.text: Horseman at end of night getting smashed!

indicators.note: end of picks out the final letter of night
getting smashed means the preceding letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A rider at the close of a night out gets very drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of HORSEMAN, AT and T (the last letter of night) are rearranged. Burns's Tam o' Shanter rides home drunk late at night, so the whole clue also describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns's poem tells of a farmer riding home drunk at night, chased by witches.

clue.text: Economize on character in Shaw's first play

parts.note: re means on, concerning
Dr Harry Trench is the young hero of Widowers' Houses, Shaw's first play

explanation.surface: Someone saves money by studying a figure in Shaw's debut drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' might suggest a letter; it is a person in the play Widowers' Houses (1892).
explanation.definitionFit: To cut back on spending is to economize.

clue.text: Apologetic address directed at one such as Euterpe about start of ode

parts.note: to means directed at
a means one

indicators.note: about means the muse word goes around the next letter

parts.note: Euterpe is one of the nine Muses, so she is a muse

indicators.note: start of takes the first letter of ode

explanation.surface: A poet humbly invokes a Muse at the opening of a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns's poem To a Mouse apologises to the creature whose nest his plough destroyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns's poem is addressed to a field creature and opens by apologising for wrecking its nest.

clue.text: Miss Golightly's friend Sally is a real fruit!

definitions.meaning: Sally ... is the jailed gangster Holly Golightly visits in Breakfast at Tiffany's
botanically the salad vegetable is in fact a fruit

explanation.definitionFit: The gangster's surname in Capote's novella is also the red salad plant botanists class as a fruit.

clue.text: You're a dirtylittle schoolboy.' 'Besides bein'- immoral'" (Stalky & Co)

definitions.text: You're a dirtylittle schoolboy.' 'Besides bein'- immoral'" (Stalky & Co)

parts.words: You're a dirtylittle schoolboy.' 'Besides bein'- immoral'" (Stalky & Co)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Kipling's school stories, with the missing adverb marked by the dash

explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from 'frabjous', coined in Jabberwocky; Kipling's boys pick it up as slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is Lewis Carroll's coinage meaning joyously, used jokingly by Kipling's schoolboys.

clue.text: A memorial evening on which to enjoy eating and drinking, unless the chef does

definitions.text: A memorial evening on which to enjoy eating and drinking
definitions.meaning: the 25th January dinner honouring Scotland's national poet
read as a sentence, the cook spoiling the meal by overcooking it

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase into a cook who chars the evening meal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish dinner commemorating the poet Robert Burns is held each January with haggis and whisky.

clue.text: Bespectacled pirate who's meek, somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A gentle buccaneer wearing glasses is a little mild.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Hook's bosun in Peter Pan is the pirate who wears spectacles.

clue.text: Prepare a cane for beating? Encore!

indicators.note: for beating means the letters are battered into a new order

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster readies the cane, and the punishment comes again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Encore' is the call for a performer to return, so the answer is the performer coming back.
explanation.definitionFit: An encore is a further appearance by a performer after the show seems over.

clue.text: Supplies commentary as Atonement's confused, but not me!

indicators.note: confused shows that letters are jumbled together, here with some letters taken away

parts.note: Atonement is Ian McEwan's novel; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A critic adds notes to McEwan's muddled novel but leaves himself out.
explanation.walkthrough: Mix the letters of AS ATONEMENT; 'but not me' says that once ME is taken out the remaining nine letters give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To add explanatory notes to a text is to provide a commentary on it.

clue.text: What's done with the remainders of Bring Up the Bodies?

definitions.text: What's done with the remainders of Bring Up the Bodies?

parts.words: What's done with the remainders of Bring Up the Bodies?
parts.note: remainders are unsold books, but here it plays on remains, the bodies being put back in the ground

explanation.walkthrough: Bring Up the Bodies is Hilary Mantel's novel; 'bring up' suggests exhumation, answered by putting bodies back.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting remains back into the earth a second time is interment again.

clue.text: At start of Salome rashly takes notice and buys one to go regularly to Covent Garden

definitions.text: one to go regularly to Covent Garden

indicators.note: at start of takes the opening letter of Salome
rashly means the following words are thrown hastily into a new order

explanation.surface: An opera lover, seeing Salome, impulsively commits to attending the Royal Opera House often.
explanation.walkthrough: Covent Garden is the home of London's Royal Opera House, where Strauss's Salome is staged.
explanation.definitionFit: A pass valid for a whole series of performances lets the holder attend repeatedly.

clue.text: Author of Rhinoceros, carelessly omitting first two parts right out

definitions.text: Author of Rhinoceros, carelessly omitting first two parts right out

indicators.note: carelessly means the remaining letters are tossed into a new order
right out means the letter standing for right is removed
omitting first two parts drops the opening pair of letters of the play title

explanation.surface: A playwright's work is sloppily cut, its opening and a correction thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: From RHINOCEROS drop RH ('omitting first two parts') and an R ('right out'), leaving INOCEOS to rearrange. Eugène Ionesco wrote the absurdist play Rhinoceros.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romanian-French absurdist dramatist wrote the 1959 play about townsfolk turning into rhinos.

clue.text: What you might eat at 12, a type of fish with pith mostly

parts.note: the hag, or hagfish, is an eel-like sea creature

indicators.note: mostly means the word for pith loses its last letter

parts.note: the gist of something is its pith or essence

explanation.surface: A meal recommendation names a kind of fish served with most of its pith.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 refers to the answer at 12-down, the January dinner for Burns, where this pudding is the centrepiece.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiced sheep's-offal pudding is the traditional main dish at the Scottish poet's anniversary dinner.

clue.text: One's outstandingly impressive pop singer and femme fatale

definitions.meaning: slang for a remarkable person or thing, a corker
the Scottish pop star of Shout, and the seductive heroine of Berg's opera

explanation.definitionFit: The slang word for a humdinger is also the stage name of a Scottish pop star and Berg's seductress.

clue.text: Giving colour, note, to new actor I cast at end of revival

parts.note: ti is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: cast means the letters are thrown into a different arrangement
at end of takes the final letter of revival

explanation.surface: A theatre note about casting a new actor at the close of a revival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like theatre casting but signals the rearrangement of ACTOR I into CTORIA.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to dyeing, imparting hue or tint to a material.

clue.text: One such as Krapp to fade away

definitions.meaning: Krapp in Beckett's Krapp's Last Tape records himself on tape every year

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who records tapes describes Beckett's Krapp, and to dwindle gradually is to thin out.

clue.text: In Germinal impetuous hanger-on

indicators.note: in says the answer lies inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A character in Zola's novel is an impulsive sponger.
explanation.walkthrough: Germinal is Émile Zola's novel of a mining strike.
explanation.definitionFit: The shellfish clings tight to rocks, so the word figuratively means a clinging follower.

clue.text: A Freudian construct is certain to include exercises and a game

indicators.note: to include means the first word wraps around the next piece

parts.note: sure means certain
PE is physical education, school exercises
go is the Japanese board game

explanation.surface: A psychoanalytic idea is said to involve gym work and a match.
explanation.definitionFit: In Freud's model of the mind this is the conscience-like part that sets moral standards.

clue.text: Note start of play in theatre

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

indicators.note: start of takes the first letter of play

explanation.surface: A remark about the opening of a stage production.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for repertory, a company or playhouse staging a rotating programme of plays.

clue.text: "Mr. Woodhouse was safely conveyed in his carriage … to partake of this —— party (Emma)

definitions.text: "Mr. Woodhouse was safely conveyed in his carriage … to partake of this —— party (Emma)

parts.words: "Mr. Woodhouse was safely conveyed in his carriage … to partake of this —— party (Emma)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Jane Austen's Emma, the dash marking the missing words that describe an outdoor party

explanation.walkthrough: The scene is the outing to Donwell Abbey, where the hypochondriac Mr Woodhouse is carefully brought along.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing phrase means in the open air, describing the strawberry-picking party at Donwell Abbey.

clue.text: 12, say, that's just about gone

parts.note: re means about or concerning
past means gone by

explanation.surface: A reference to a Scottish dinner that has only just ended.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 refers to the answer at 12-down, the dinner for Burns, which is an example of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A Burns Supper is an example of a meal, which is the meaning of this formal word.
